maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT RESPECTING ARRANGEMENTS FOR OPENING CEREMONIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT RESPECTING ARRANGEMENTS FOR OPENING CEREMONIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to make a statement concerning the ceremonies arranged for the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway. You will recall that some days ago a question was asked concerning these ceremonies. At that time I stated that as soon as arrangements had been made between the Canadian and United States governments an announcement would be made. Today an announcement similar to the one I am about to make will emanate from the White House in Washington.
President Eisenhower has accepted an invitation to come to Canada to join Her Majesty the Queen in these ceremonies. He will arrive on June 26. The ceremonies will take place at the St. Lambert lock near Montreal. The President of the United States and Mrs. Eisenhower will fly from Washington to Montreal on the morning of June 26 and will join Her Majesty and Prince Philip on the royal yacht Britannia for the purpose of jointly contributing to the opening ceremonies. The details of the program are being worked out by officials of the Canadian and United States governments. After the opening ceiemonies at Montreal the royal yacht will proceed through the lock and thence to the great lakes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT RESPECTING ARRANGEMENTS FOR OPENING CEREMONIES
speechtext:
May I tell the Prime Minister that this is very welcome news indeed. I hasten to extend to him and to the government our congratulations upon the success which has been experienced in getting the President of the United States to join Her Majesty the Queen in recognizing the national as well as the international aspect of the St. Lawrence seaway, namely in its opening in the city of Montreal, where it enters into the province of Quebec, and then its continuation in the international section both in the state of New York and in the province of Ontario.
I think all of us will welcome the announcement. I am delighted at it personally, as I am sure will be the citizens of Montreal as well as those who live in the international
section. I cannot tell the Prime Minister how happy I am at this decision.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT RESPECTING ARRANGEMENTS FOR OPENING CEREMONIES
speechtext:
The announcement made today demonstrates that it is possible for Canada and the United States to work together for the good of both countries on a major economic project. It is indeed a happy occasion for Canada that Her Majesty, along with President Eisenhower of the United States, should be coming to officiate at the opening of this very important undertaking.
I think this must also be a particularly happy occasion for the hon. member for Laurier who himself played such an important role in initiating this major undertaking and supervising the work for a number of years. I express the hope that the plans for a joint parliamentary delegation to meet about that time will have the same successful results as the announcement indicates today in another way.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STATEMENT RESPECTING ARRANGEMENTS FOR OPENING CEREMONIES
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Assiniboia for their words. On this occasion, when the House of Commons is so much in agreement, I should like, if I may, to bring one further matter to the attention of hon. members and the country. That is that Her Majesty, having regard to the tremendous nature of this project and the desirability of honouring those who made a contribution thereto, those often remaining anonymous, has graciously suggested that as a mark of recognition a book be compiled containing the names of all workmen and others who were employed on the construction of this project or who contributed to the building of the seaway, extending honour to them individually and at the same time recognizing the dignity and the responsibility of those who in their daily toil make such a contribution to our country and the preservation of our way of life.

subtopic: TEXTILES-TABLING OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON COTTONS

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TEXTILES-TABLING OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON COTTONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies in English and in French of a report I have received from the chairman of the tariff board relating to reference No. 125 on textiles. I am also tabling a transcript of

Tabling of Report
the evidence presented to the board at its public hearings. I think I should interject here that I commend the reading of this transcript to my hon. friends opposite.
This report deals with cotton and cotton products. It is the tariff board's third report pursuant to reference No. 125. Earlier reports dealt with wool fabrics and with certain wool yarns and textile wastes. Subsequent reports will cover synthetic textile fabrics and manufactures, woollen apparel, knitted goods and other textile products.
The board's hearings on cotton and cotton products were lengthy, 48 days in all, and the evidence was voluminous. However, the report is quite compact. It comprises two small volumes, of which the second is a statistical appendix. The conclusions and recommendations are summarized in volume 1 of the report on pages 111 to 121.
The tariff board found that the two great divisions of the Canadian textile industry which process natural fibres-wool and cotton-have much in common. Both use imported raw material; both rely to a considerable extent upon female labour; both are long established in Canada; both are keenly affected by import competition and by competition from man-made fibres, and both are vulnerable to the whims of fashion.
It was also found, however, that there are important differences between these two important branches of the textile industry. By and large, woollens constitute a town or village industry; cottons, for the most part, are produced in metropolitan areas. Taken as a whole, the Canadian cotton industry was found to be in a much healthier state financially than its counterpart producing woollens and worsteds.
The Canadian primary cotton industry's most serious problems stem in large part, it was found, from the ever-changing variety in pattern, colour and finish of fabrics demanded by its customers; and from the presence on its very threshold of the most modern, the most diversified and the most aggressive cotton cloth industry in the world, that of the United States. The board concludes, however, that by and large our industry is standing up to the competition. That the Canadian cotton industry has been able to hold the domestic market to the extent it has done is, in the board's words, "a tribute to its initiative, its efficiency and its adaptability in the face of circumstances which it dare not ignore and which, for the most part, it is powerless to alter".
The board states that in undertaking the formulation of a draft tariff schedule, as it was directed to do by my letter of reference,

it kept in mind the desirability of revising a schedule which has been little changed in 30 years; of deleting from the tariff such items as have lost their significance; of simplifying and modernizing the terminology; of reducing as far as possible the number of classifications; and of giving due consideration to the effect that changes in rates might have upon consumers and upon secondary industries using cotton yarns or fabrics.
Under the proposed new cotton schedule recommended by the board some 50 existing tariff classifications would be reduced to 20. This consolidation would involve increases in some rates and reductions in others. The remaining items would be regrouped and the terminology simplified. All of the duties would be on an ad valorem basis.
The board states that the proposed schedule provides for a small increase in protection for Canadian cotton yarn spinners; very little change as regards the thread industry, and moderate increases in most favoured nation rates in respect of bleached fabrics and coloured fabrics. With regard to item 523b, the important item which covers most coloured fabrics, a simple ad valorem most favoured nation rate of 224 per cent would be introduced according to the board's recommendations. The present most favoured nation rates range from 17J Per cent plus 3 cents per pound to 25 per cent plus 34 cents per pound, depending on the value of the fabric. The British preferential rate would remain unchanged at 174 per cent. I should like to add that the British preferential rates show little change throughout the revised schedule as proposed by the board, and that such changes as do occur are incidental to the revision of classifications and descriptions of goods.
From what I have said it will be clear that to implement the recommendations would involve numerous changes, some upward and some downward. Many of the rates of duty which would be affected are now bound under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. Hon. members will appreciate, accordingly, that GATT negotiations would be involved if the board's recommendations were to be implemented, and such negotiations normally occupy a matter of months. I should also point out that if such negotiations were undertaken they might involve the further reports on textiles which I hope to receive later this year from the tariff board.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare arising out of the great interest taken by the Canadian people in obtaining a cure for cancer.
Has the statement by Dr. Gordon Murray, who has developed a serum for use in the treatment of cancer, in which he requests federal and provincial public health departments to do research work toward the development of a cancer vaccine, been brought to the attention of the minister; and can the minister say whether action is being taken by the federal government to expand cancer research?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monieilh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DR. MURRAY  REQUEST FOR PUBLIC HEALTH RESEARCH INTO CANCER VACCINE
speechtext:
I should like to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of this question. I have followed closely and with great interest the reports which have been issued on the serum developed by Dr. Gordon Murray of Toronto in his research aimed at the production of an anti-cancer vaccine, and my attention has been directed to his most recent statement on his further experience with this serum.
Regarding the second part of the question, whether action is being taken by the federal government to expand cancer research, I can say quite definitely that action has already been taken both by the federal and provincial governments and the national agency directly concerned, the national cancer institute, to expand progressively research in this field. At the time of its organization it was felt desirable in the interests of encouraging the highest level of research performance that the national cancer institute should be the agency, on a country-wide basis, to coordinate this specific research effort, and for its experts to appraise and assess the requests for assistance in cancer studies.
To stimulate in a tangible way the development of this program the federal government, under the national health grants, together with a number of provincial governments, provide annual contributions to the national cancer institute's research resources. Since the beginning of the national health grants program the federal government has provided from the cancer grant a total of about $1,100,000 to supplement funds directly available to the institute. This amount has been matched by contributions from the provinces.
An indication of the growth of the program of the national cancer institute is the fact that their total appropriation for the year 1948 was $87,400, whereas their most recent budget, that is for 1958-59, totalled $1,024,000.
When in the opinion of the experts associated with the institute and other prominent research leaders in Canada this serum has been developed to a state of assuring positive benefit to those afflicted with cancer, as in the case of any discovery which offers reasonable promise of improving health and controlling disease-for example, as the poliomyelitis vaccine immunization program-the federal government will spare no effort to bring the benefit of such discoveries to the Canadian people.

Inquiries of the Ministry or domestic use. This procedure is in accordance with the authority granted under the Canadian wheat board regulations 195859 crop year, part II, paragraph 6, subparagraph (1), approved by order in council P.C. 1958-725.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention at all to add unduly to the length of the debate that took place last Friday when this item came up for consideration.
I was here in the house last Friday, and the C.B.C. strike had then reached its 40th day. I heard the speeches made by members from both sides of the house, and particularly by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) and by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). Mr. Chairman, early in the afternoon of last Friday, the Minister of National Revenue made the following statement to the house, as reported on page 775 of Hansard:
I was waiting, Mr. Chairman, to see whether hon. members had anything else to say on this estimate before it was carried.
And the Minister of National Revenue went on to say:
It is an extremely difficult situation in which I find myself this afternoon. As hon. members well know, negotiations are going on at this very moment, or at least I hope so. They started at 12 o'clock and I trust that if they have concluded it will be in a satisfactory way.
Well, Mr. Chairman, on Friday the Minister of National Revenue stated that he was expecting to hear at any moment of the settlement of the C.B.C. strike. Shortly afterwards I saw the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Chambers) enter the

house, and send a page over to the Minister of National Revenue with a message. I thought, as did all my colleagues, that the C.B.C. strike was ended or was on the verge of settlement. Now, like all members of the federal government and particularly those whose constituencies are affected by the C.B.C. strike, I have received many letters from my constituents asking me to raise the matter in the house and to ask the government-
How many letters?
Let us see them.
How many letters?
-asking me to raise the matter in the house and to ask the government to face its responsibility. However, Mr. Chairman, I refrained from doing so until today.
How many letters?

Last Friday, in view of the hon. minister's statement, we were under the impression that the strike was near settlement. And today, Mr. Chairman, on this 44th day of the strike, we hear that not only the C.B.C. strike is not settled, but that it is not likely to be settled because it seems that there is more and more beating about the bush on an extremely difficult problem.
Mr. Chairman, I rise today, on this 44th day of the strike, to ask again to the government to face its responsibilities about the C.B.C. strike, because the longer the strike lasts the more we shall hear of unjustified and unjustifiable criticism from all sources about the C.B.C. board of directors or about the C.B.C. producers.
At the beginning of this strike, the government could have seen to it that both parties met immediately and discuss between themselves the necessary steps to settle the strike. Each day we read in the papers, whether in the form of open letters to the editors or signed articles, of criticism against the C.B.C. or the producers, and the longer the strike lasts, the more significant those criticisms will become, and the more they will harm the C.B.C.'s operations and reputation.
Mr. Chairman, 74 television producers are on strike. They are supported by 1,200 employees. All they asked was not at all a salary increase, as some hon. members to the right would want us to believe, but the right to negotiate with the C.B.C. authorities.
The Minister of National Revenue stated that he was not anxious to intervene in the C.B.C. strike, that it was not part of his function and at the same time, Mr. Chairman, he declared that the strike was illegal. There-
Supply-C.B.C.
fore, I submit with great respect that in declaring the strike illegal, the Minister of National Revenue was intervening in the C.B.C. strike, but not in the way he should have.
Since then, Mr. Chairman, public opinion has been split in two camps; even the cabinet has been split in two camps. The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) said that the strike was legal, and the Minister of National Revenue said it was not. The Minister of Labour has followed the policy of the ostrich, which buries its head in the sand so as not to see what is going on around it.
Well, Mr. Chairman, public opinion is split in two groups and so is the government. The strike is now in its 44th day and we are no farther ahead than on the first day; indeed we are perhaps farther than we think from an equitable solution.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, who is in the house at this moment, has done his best to settle the strike; he has tried to bring both parties together so that the strike might be settled. Mr. Chairman, I have much regard and admiration for the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George who tried-although the Minister of National Revenue would not see it that way

to find a solution to the C.B.C. producers' strike. And I find he deserves much sympathy in that he was not more openly supported by our hon. friends opposite.
Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George can act as a mediator or referee between both parties, is it not the duty of the Minister of National Revenue himself, who answers for the expenditures and management of the C.B.C., to intervene so as to find a referee? If the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George lacks his government's support and if, as the Minister of National Revenue said, he is taking those steps on his own, of his own free will, I am of the opinion that the Canadian people are entitled to expect a different stand on the part of the government under which the C.B.C. is controlled and administered.
Attempts have been made in articles or short pieces a la Rumilly-what we call back home "Rumilliades"-in articles published in certain newspapers like the one I have here, for instance, to discredit the C.B.C. producers and the government itself.
Mr. Chairman, the longer the strike lasts, the longer you will have the opportunity of reading such vicious, biased and nefarious articles, whole pages of them, from the pens of friends of the Union Nationale, like Mr. Robert Rumilly, who misses no opportunity to indulge in shallow politicizing to the detriment of our national endeavours.

Supply-C.B.C.
As a matter of fact, while the C.B.C. is labouring under an untenable situation, Mr. Robert Rumilly is jumping at the chance to shower compliments on the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), who deserves them, of course, since he thinks like Mr. Rumilly; in fact, he dreams of him, he "rumillizes" all day long, so to speak.
And then, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Rumilly went so far as to write the following:
Is it not the right moment for the provincial government to set up the Quebec broadcasting corporation which has been desired and announced for so long?
Well, Mr. Chairman, that Quebec radio corporation, that Quebec TV corporation will never exist, but the C.B.C. does exist. The Minister of National Revenue therefore has a duty to intervene, and he is responsible for anything that develops by way of national disunity and blots the C.B.C.'s record. The full responsibility rests on the Minister of National Revenue and on the Minister of Labour, who is now looking at me, and who also has his share of responsibility, though he seems unaware of it.
Like the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), I should like to refer to section 56, subsection 1 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which, in my view, can never be mentioned often enough. In fact, the more this section is referred to, the less the Minister of Labour is willing to explain his attitude.
Here is what is provided in section 56, subsection 1 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act:
The Minister may either upon application or of his own initiative, where he deems it expedient, make or cause to be made any inquiries he thinks fit regarding industrial matters, and may do such things as seem calculated to maintain or secure industrial peace and to promote conditions favourable to settlement of disputes.
In spite of the authority vested in him by that section, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Labour buries his head in the sand and sees nothing. Moreover, while the act clearly states that the Minister of National Revenue must concern himself with the administration of the C.B.C., he says he has nothing to do with this strike.
Mr. Chairman, nearly five million listeners of the French network of the C.B.C. are deploring this situation, are pained by it, and are clamouring for the government to intervene; yet the government refuses to accept its responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, television is no luxury, it is not an instrument to be trusted to the hands of Mr. Rumilly or of the member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. Television is an important organization way above the people we heard mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, television today is a training school for the general public, for our people of all ages and all classes who are constant spectators of this modern invention. Television is no longer a luxury, and this medium which has become the day to day companion of five to six million listeners of the French network, is offering us just now certain shows which are not interesting, because they were not meant for us.
C.B.C. producers are entitled to expect something else than insults from certain newspapermen of the "Rumilly" type and we ourselves should expect something else than to see producers' names used at every turn, to hear discussions on their account in and out of season, and to read biased, libellous, slanderous and dishonest articles about them, such as we have seen in open letters published by certain official newspapers.
The C.B.C. producers are a group of distinguished, cultured, able and sincere men who have a right to press their demands. They have the right to negotiate with their employer, as have all other classes of society. We find now that these valuable men are being disparaged.
As the Minister of National Revenue said last Friday, the French network of the C.B.C. has become in a few years the largest of its kind in the world.
Recently, I have had the opportunity to discuss this matter with some French people from Paris who praised the manner in which C.B.C. programs are prepared, and they even added that the French radio of Paris could learn a great deal from the French network of the C.B.C.
Mr. Chairman, if I rise in my place today, it is not to side with the C.B.C. board of governors, or with the C.B.C. producers; but I am sick and tired like the whole population of the province of Quebec, of hearing so-called rightist people or newspapermen slander C.B.C. authorities or C.B.C. producers. Both the management and the producers of the C.B.C. deserve congratulations for having managed, thanks to their close co-operation over the years, to direct and develop from scratch the finest French T.V. network in the world. If the C.B.C. board of governors deserves congratulations, so do the producers, for all those years during which they worked together in the best spirit of understanding. This cleavage between employers and producers does no good to either group and certainly does no good to the government, especially if we consider its attitude toward that problem.
Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. must absolutely work out a settlement of that strike; and unless the board of governors co-operates, settlement is impossible. What is unthinkable

is that the C.B.C. board of governors should be deprived of its producers any longer.
What we see reminds us of a body without a soul. Mr. Chairman, once again, after the hon. members for Laurier, St. Denis, Dollard (Messrs. Chevrier, Denis, Rouleau) and all those who have expressed their opinion freely and frankly in the house, I urge the government and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) to intervene immediately. Let them stop passing the buck and shoulder their responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, this is all I want to say but I can never too emphatically tell the government and the minister that they cannot evade the responsibility they have of intervening in the C.B.C. strike. On behalf of millions of people who are paying taxes for the privilege of hearing and seeing first-class programs on the dominion radio and television networks, we have a right to ask for the immediate settlement of the strike and the intervention of the government in this dispute.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped to catch your eye before the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville, and I might have been able to save him the necessity of making his heated appeal or the necessity, at any rate, of making all of it.
I think it might be useful to the house if I should state at this time what the situation is in the negotiations that are going on between the C.B.C. and certain sections of their employees in Montreal. In the first place, as most hon. members know, there have been prolonged negotiations because we were faced with a difficult situation in which both sides had taken positions which they believed in strongly and it was difficult to reconcile them. However, we have made some progress. I can tell the committee that while nothing has been signed, a solution has been found to the problem that existed between the producers and the C.B.C.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Is the hon. member now making a statement on behalf of the government?

No; I am not making a
statement on behalf of the government. I am making a statement on my own behalf as
Supply-C.B.C.
the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George on a situation with which I happen to be acquainted and in which I think the committee will be interested. I have had no instructions-and I should like to make that point clear-from any member of the government in this matter whatsoever. In fact, I do not think that hon. members would suggest that it would be proper for the government to give me instructions in this matter. I do not feel at liberty to outline the actual agreements that have been reached at this time because, as I say, they have not been signed and they are not necessarily binding on anyone.
The situation that exists is this. I believe that a formula has been found to settle this difference but the producers in Montreal do not feel that they can sign a settlement until the people who respected their picket lines are satisfied that they can return to work under conditions that will keep their members happy. Hence we have a situation where five other groups which have been respecting these picket lines are approaching the C.B.C. to find out whether they can receive certain guarantees. The C.B.C. at the same time has contracts negotiated in the past with these groups and all on the national level.
One of the complicating factors is that some of the groups in Montreal have had differences of opinion with their national officers. The national officers in some cases have not supported the strike and the Montreal locals have respected the picket lines. You have the difficulty here in that the C.B.C. feels obliged to deal with people with whom they have contracts and the people in Montreal feel that perhaps they would not be properly represented if they dealt along that line. A solution to that problem has not been found. There is also the matter of the actual terms under which these people will return to work; I refer to the people who have been respecting the picket lines. Hence the problems have become bound up with each other.
I believe that a solution will be found. Exactly when that will happen is hard to say, but meetings are going on between the various people in an effort to find a solution to this secondary problem. As I say, I believe that a solution has been found to the first problem. But the signing of that solution or the document representing that solution is delayed until the other groups which have been involved in this matter reach an agreement, you might say, with the C.B.C. I do

Supply-C.B.C.
not believe that too much help will be given to these continuing negotiations by newspaper stories or speeches in the house that strongly take one side or the other. We have an amicable feeling existing. I should like to pay tribute to the people on both sides for their patience, their good faith and their real willingness to find a solution. That situation still exists. With that feeling existing, I am sure that the parties will get together.
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I recognize the Leader of the Opposition.

If the Leader of the Opposition is rising to speak in the debate, Mr. Chairman, may I say that, in all fairness, I think the floor should be given to a member of the C.C.F. group at this time in keeping with the practice.
No.

If the Leader of the Opposition insists, I will yield. I think it is a long established practice to follow the procedure I have suggested.
I listened to the statement made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George with a great deal of interest. I think that anything that any hon. member of this house can do to bring about an amicable settlement at the earliest possible moment is something to be commended.
Hear, hear.

Before the applause gets too loud, may I say this. The question that I should like to have answered is this: where does the government fit in with respect to this whole important dispute? We have had this strike going on now for some six weeks, I believe. I do not believe that in recent years there has been debated in this house any subject about which members of parliament felt more strongly than they do about this particular situation that now exists. They feel strongly about the lack of French language programs of the quality and type of those that the producers have been putting forward for many years. This strike has denied to five million French speaking Canadians these programs which are dear to them.
I listened to the speech made by the hon. member for Laurier last Friday. To me it was a moving speech, and I think he was perfectly justified in coming back again and again to the point that this government should 
do everything possible to bring about a just settlement in this dispute at an early date. We have had by this government an exhibition that I can scarcely remember ever having been equalled in this chamber. The government has spoken on this question-as I have already said on a previous occasion- in at least three different ways. The Minister of National Revenue has stated in strong language that, in his opinion, the strike was illegal. He was not satisfied with that statement. On another occasion, according to reports, he went on to say that the strike was silly and to use other adjectives of that type. Then we have had the statement of the Solicitor General who, I would think is a man well versed in the law, occupying that important position in the cabinet and no doubt tendering advice of a legal nature to his colleagues from time to time. He has been most consistent in saying that the strike is legal. You have there, Mr. Chairman, two opposite opinions.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
Is the hon. member aware that the musicians union have declared the strike to be illegal and have instructed their members to continue to work?
Oh, oh.

What an inference there is in that question, Mr. Chairman, namely that the responsibility of this government for a legal opinion lies somewhere outside this chamber. This is an additional position that is being taken by members of the Conservative party.
Answer the question.

One position is that the strike is legal. The other is that it is illegal. The Minister of Labour says, "I do not know and I am not talking". The hon. member says that some other organization outside of this house has expressed a view.
The union.

I have my own view and I am quite prepared on my responsibility to state my view. But it has nothing to do with the views that have been expressed outside this house.
We have had these three separate views from the government. We have had the state-

ment of the Minister of National Revenue that he did not wish to interfere in the strike. How could he interfere in a more direct way than to stand up in this chamber and say the strike is illegal; that is interference in the strongest possible fashion. In order to ascertain what the government is doing in this regard members of the opposition parties have addressed what I would consider to be very proper questions to the administration today concerning the progress being made. What are the answers? What has been the response of the ministers? We do not know; we have no information; or we will take it as notice. A member of the cabinet, one of Her Majesty's privy councillors, says he will take it as notice. Then, we have a private member on the government side of the house, an illustrious backbencher who has been doing his best to do the work of the government, getting up in this committee and giving us a progress report in connection with these negotiations.
I am sorry that the Minister of National Revenue cannot be here this afternoon. Of course, the same situation applies to all of us from time to time, and I have no criticism to make of him for not being here. However, I would think that when the Minister of National Revenue is away and an hon. member puts a question to the Acting Minister of National Revenue there should be no hesitation on the government side of the house as to who is Acting as Minister of National Revenue. When I addressed that question to the government there was a strange silence; there was a strange immobility. Finally, after a long silence, the hon. member for Greenwood caught the ball and said he would take it as notice. Here we are waiting for the government to say what progress is being made in the settlement of this strike, and I think parliament is entitled at this time to a report from a responsible minister. According to the Ottawa Citizen of Friday, January 30, the Minister of National Revenue has made a very strong statement in connection with this regrettable affair. He said, according to the report on page five of the Citizen of that date, under the heading "Nowlan Seeks Union For Cabinet":
Revenue Minister Nowlan was guest speaker at the annual banquet of the customs and excise officers association held at the Eastview recreation centre.
In an address frequently punctuated with humour, Mr. Nowlan declared that the C.B.C. producers strike was "unfortunate and frankly very silly. Someone should organize a union of cabinet ministers".
Supply-C.B.C.
The minister says in the house that he is not interfering in the strike. The minister says that someone should try to organize a union for the cabinet.
There may be difficulty in that case in getting certification for that particular group.

I might say it would be very difficult to get the cabinet members themselves to agree on the terms of any contract or any union they might wish to form. The Minister of National Revenue would say that a union for the cabinet is illegal. The Solicitor General would say it is legal, and when they went to the man who is the authority on labour matters, the Minister of Labour, he would say, I don't know. Then, of course, we would refer it to some of the backbenchers who would take action to solicit the cabinet ministers one by one to see if they were interested in forming such a union. Then, of course, they would take statements from people outside the house to see what their program should be.
This cabinet has been here for only 17 months, and look at the many directions in which they are now going. In so far as the Minister of Labour is concerned, he has played a very constructive role in many of the labour disputes in the past. He should use his good offices today to help these parties arrive at a satisfactory conclusion to this dispute. However, I can understand why he is so careful not to make a comment when there is such a division in the cabinet on this very important and very aggravating question.
I have read the remarks of the Minister of National Revenue in this house last Friday. In that statement he said many things with which I can agree. Perhaps I should quote his exact words from page 777 of Hansard for February 6, 1959:
This was a government which was going to wreck the C.B.C. This was a government which would interfere with the C.B.C. It is rather ironic, Mr. Chairman, that the minister who was so diligent in making sure there was no interference with the C.B.C. in any way, shape or form, is now being criticized because he has refused to intervene in this matter.
How can he make that statement-I am quite willing to say that this could be an error-when it is so much in conflict with other statements in this house concerning this dispute. Then he went on to say, farther on, that interference with the C.B.C. was different from interference with the Canadian National Railways because:
-if it once became a political football or a subject of political interference could be wrecked.
Those are exactly the sentiments of members of the C.C.F. We feel that there should

Supply-C.B.C.
be no political interference with the C.B.C. in any way, but we suggest it is political interference for the Minister of National Revenue to comment that the strike is illegal and to have used words to the effect that the strike was unfortunate and frankly very silly.
I am hopeful that the government will, even at this late hour, use the good offices of the Minister of Labour to see if a settlement cannot be obtained. I have read the reference to the matter in the Toronto Star of February 10 and referred to the fact a strike ballot is being taken among 1,400 technicians in the nationwide English network. I am hopeful that there will be no spreading of this strike. I am hopeful that it will be settled today, but I ask the government to reconsider its whole position and to take action to use the good offices of the Minister of Labour to bring about a fair settlement.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to detain the committee very long; especially do I not desire to stand in the way of the observations that my hon. friend seated behind me wishes to make. We on this side, Mr. Chairman, have argued that a major characteristic of the policy and attitude of this government has been confusion and contradiction, and it seems to me that it has in no way been better illustrated or displayed than in this particular situation which we are discussing at this moment.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George by his intervention I think in a sense also illustrated that confusion. I do not, of course, criticize him in any way, shape or form for the effort which he had been making, as a private member of the house on the government side, to bring this dispute to a satisfactory conclusion. I commend him for what he has tried to do, as, indeed, I would commend any hon. member in this house who intervened constructively in this dispute. The hon. member has made a report to the committee on his activities in this regard, and it was a report which I suggest, Mr. Chairman, might have come with even greater effect from someone who was authorized to speak for the government. The hon. member has indicated in his report that a draft agreement has been drawn up between the two parties most concerned, and that in his opinion the solution might well be reached very soon. We all hope, of course, that that will be the case. But if 1 took down the words of the hon. member correctly, he added that this draft agreement of which he talked was not necessarily binding, and he went on to explain that the difficulty now in reaching a final and satisfactory solution is in the relationship of this draft agreement to certain

unions who have been concerned with the issue in an important capacity. That, Mr. Chairman, surely underlines what we have been arguing on this side, namely that the government should have intervened. Because there can surely be no doubt about the propriety of government intervention and interest in a dispute which is now, as the hon. member himself indicated, one of major concern to certain unions as well as to the C.B.C.
The contradictions of government policy, or the lack of policy in this matter, have been so clearly outlined by previous speakers, including my hon. friend the member for Assiniboia, that I do not need to spend any time on that topic. We are not suggesting that the government should interfere in any maimer whatsoever with the operation of the C.B.C. That would be quite improper, and is something, of course, to be guarded against. But we are suggesting, and we have been suggesting for some days now, that the government should have intervened in a labour dispute which may have far-reaching consequences beyond the limits of a strictly labour dispute. Of course, in that intervention the government does not need to take any position, and should not take any position, in regard to the substance of the dispute. But I do suggest what the hon. member for Assiniboia, and other members before him, have already suggested, and that is that the government has already by its attitude taken a position in this matter. There comes a time when non-intervention can be intervention, and that position, I suggest, has been reached in this matter. It is easy to explain the reason for refusing to intervene formally in this matter, as some members of the government have done, in terms which condemn one side to the dispute and not the other. That is a form of non-intervention which is intervening in the wrong way.
The hon. Minister of Labour, who is, or should be, the minister most concerned in this matter as a labour minister, cannot be getting any satisfaction whatever from the continuance of this dispute which has now, I think, gone on for 44 days. He is, as we all know, a sincere, indeed a very generous-minded minister, and I am sure that he regrets, as we all regret, the damage that has been done already by this dispute. I am sure that he is just as worried as we are about the implication of the failure to settle this issue shortly. Surely even now at this late date, which is the 44th day of the dispute, the Minister of Labour will reconsider his position and initiate those conciliation procedures which are at his disposal in an effort to bring this dispute to a speedy and successful conclusion and I suggest that all the resources of his department should now be

brought to bear upon this issue to supplement the constructive activity of a private member of this house so that we, in all parties, may very shortly be able to congratulate ourselves that at last this dispute has been brought to an end.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, since the opening of the session, I have followed with great interest the zeal with which the Liberals, on the one hand, and the C.C.F.'s, on the other, have tried to spread the confusion that exists within their own ranks, and to make of this C.B.C. strike a problem which, in itself, leaves the great majority of the French speaking population of Quebec cold.
Shame!

I should like, this afternoon, without committing in any way the responsibility of my colleagues, express the opinion of my electors in the constituency of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere most of whom-as I said a moment ago-feel indifferent about that strike.
I now refer to an article which Mr. Gerard Filion, managing director of Le Devoir, is said to have written on January 31, 1959, and which may be summarized as follows:
"This strike will teach us, we hope, a lesson in modesty". Many people who thought themselves indispensable are now on their way to oblivion. The public is not very much nostalgic about television. A survey made by the students ot the College Sainte-Marie among 200 families shows that 60 per cent of those families are not suffering at all from the strike. Thirty-four per cent are suffering a little, and 6 per cent are really suffering. The same survey shows that "60 per cent have replied that the strike had made them realize that they could do without T.V. much easier than they thought".
"This is excellent news," concluded Mr. Filion.
The strike, Mr. Chairman, has given the people of Quebec the impression of being rid of certain hot-headed and leftist individuals, including the leader of the Quebec Social Democratic Party (a party without a doctrine), Michel Chartrand. We have a chance to enjoy relief from the Jeremiads of Jean Marchand, Rene Levesque, Andre Laurendeau and Gerard Filion.
And of Jean Lesage.
The people of Quebec can now see films of real educational value which largely make up for the platitudinous programs we are given on many occasions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
So, you like going to Paris?
Supply-C.B.C.

No. I do not live in Paris, I live in the province of Quebec-and you, Liberal gentlemen, you have laid the groundwork for and supported that strike. Why? Because the key posts are held by your proteges.
And when the producers and artists staged a march on Ottawa, what did we see? We saw the member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and the head of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Argue) going out to meet them.
What about the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion)?
Are you jealous?

No, I am not jealous. A moment ago the member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) said he has received sheaves of letters. Well, so have I received letters, and I have been asked not to take up the matter with the government and to let the problem settle itself.
Mr. Chairman, it is about time that the people of Quebec had the opportunity-and there is now an opportunity-to rid themselves of Andre Laurendeau, editor-in-chief of Le Devoir, who in an article which appeared on February 22, enquired whether there were any Conservative members in this House of Commons. It is time that the people be rid of Andre Laurendeau, whose daughter delighted in strike duty in front of the Quebec legislature, and also of Rene Levesque, Mr. Chairman, the one who went to Russia and upon his return-
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. We are now being asked to vote funds for the C.B.C. This is no time to put the various C.B.C. producers on trial one by one.
That is precisely what I was dealing with.
I would ask the hon. member to show some respect for the producers.
I shall have something to say about them in a moment-
Did you show respect for Ru-milly a moment ago?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would ask hon. members to please take their seats when the Chairman of committees rises.
I shall make my remarks both in English and in French.
In fact, we are wandering quite a bit from the motion under consideration. We have

Supply-C.B.C.
wandered too far. I must warn hon. members of the house that their speeches should relate to the motion under consideration and that any attempt to get away from the motion will be ruled out of order.
I would also ask hon. members on both sides to refrain, where possible, from discussing personalities. The debate is on the matter of a $2,193,000, vote in favour of the C.B.C. and this has little to do with the people referred to by members on both sides. (Text):
I should like to remind members of the committee that the point of relevancy applies to resolution 701. For the sake of avoiding endless repetition, such as we have had in this current debate, speeches which do not deal with the resolution from now on will be considered out of order.
(Translation):

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. When I see that today we are called upon to vote $2,193,552, I feel I am justified in arousing public opinion about the favouritism being shown towards certain C.B.C. performers.
We have heard our Liberal colleagues tell us, in a broken voice, about this strike, because they can see their pet stars facing a public reaction other than the one they had expected.
Mr. Chairman, I believe this amount of $2,193,552 should not be used to pay certain producers that I mentioned a moment ago, who unfortunately are the leaders of the C.B.C. producers while the producers themselves are the true victims of this strike and to whom I offer my heartfelt sympathy. I know that they cannot freely express their opinions because of the threats proferred by some leaders and organizers of this strike, but I hope that one day the producers who are sincere and who want to return to work, will finally be able to bring to their families what they need to lead a peaceful family life at home.
Mr. Chairman, this strike is a deplorable affair, but let us hope that common sense will finally prevail, and that once we get rid of Andre Laurendeau, Michel Chartrand, Rene Levesque, Jean Marchand and all these people, the C.B.C. strike will be settled to the satisfaction of one and all.

May I say just one word in this regard, Mr. Chairman? In the way of contradiction, this takes the cake! We have heard ministers contradict themselves, we have heard their supporters contradict themselves, we have heard one minister contradict
[The Chairman.]
himself and Conservative members contradict one another. We have heard the member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) contradict himself. He claims, all in the same breath, that we have aroused the population.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) is straying a little too much from the matter under review. May I therefore suggest that you call him to order?

Mr. Chairman, in reply to this interruption, I submit that I am not straying from the subject. In any case, I am closer to the settlement of the strike than the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) is himself. I am talking about the contradictions that have been heard-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) that we are now discussing item 701, involving an amount of $2,193,552. I therefore ask him, as well as other members, to remain within the subject under discussion.

I believe I was in order in making this statement, as I had to prove my assertions in connection with this vote. In fact, this strike has been going on for nearly two months now, and it has meant a considerable loss to the C.B.C., due to the fact that sponsors and advertisers cannot use the medium of television.
I now come back to the settlement of this strike. In my view, a settlement of this strike is a matter of public interest, even though the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) wants to have nothing to do with it and claims it is illegal. The Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) stated this afternoon that he does not want to get involved, as the matter comes under the purview of the Minister of National Revenue.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I did not say that. I have been asked to report on the negotiations and I have refused to answer that question because it is the responsibility of the Minister of National Revenue.

Mr. Chairman, I refer again to the statement of the Solicitor General. As you realize, he does not say that he did not make that statement. Therefore, I quote the words he said in this house as reported in Hansard, page 242, of the English text:
You may be assured that we are following developments very closely-

Could the Solicitor General explain to the house and to the people of Canada what he meant by "we are following developments very closely."

In answer to my hon. friend will I tell him what I mean by "we", that is, all those who are on this side of the house, and we are following the developments at this time, because we realize that the strike is a source of many difficulties for a great number of people. We are following the developments of this strike, but we are not trying to play cheap politics as our friends opposite are doing.
Does the Solicitor General feel that it is not cheap politics to deliver a speech as the one made by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere?
The policy of our friends on the other side is to criticize the C.B.C. and C.B.C. employees who owe their jobs to them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member for St. Denis when referring to a speech made by an hon. member, not to accuse him of playing cheap politics. One may qualify a speech under the political aspect, but one must not impute motives to the one who is delivering it.

Mr. Chairman, I fully agree with you, and I believe your remark is directed to the Solicitor General rather than to myself. In fact, he was the one who stated that I was indulging in cheap politics. Mr. Chairman, in reply to a question put to him about the settlement of that strike, the Solicitor General said:
Unfortunately, in the circumstances, I would not know what the future holds, and I cannot inform the house of what will happen, because the point raised is hypothetical, and I do not know what we shall be able to do in the circumstances.
This is a lot of words meaning very little. At all events, he said "I do not know", which means he is not following the matter closely. If he did, he would be aware of the situation. And if he were aware of the situation, he would know that the Minister of National Revenue does not want to deal with it. If the Solicitor General followed the matter closely, he would know that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) does not want to intervene any more than the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) wants to. Furthermore, he would also know that not a single French-speaking minister, apart from himself, has dared express an opinion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And he did not say very much.
Supply-C.B.C.
How is it that in a strike involving employees of the French network, it is an English-speaking member who defends their interests?
I rise on a point of order, I would ask the hon. member for St. Denis to withdraw what he just said.
Why?
A remark like that about a member of the house cannot be tolerated.

I said nothing insulting or
scornful about anyone.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I consider all this is out of order. Once again, I would ask the hon. members to stick to item 701, and stop this discussion which is altogether irrelevant.
(Text):
I declare out of order all present remarks and I demand all hon. members in this house to direct their discussion to item No. 701. Shall this resolution carry?
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I understand that we are called upon to vote an amount of $2,193,000 under this item. When you interrupted the member who spoke before me on a point of order, I was just reading the remarks made by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) last Friday, in which he stated:
It is an extremely difficult situation in which I find myself this afternoon. As hon. members well know, negotiations are going on at this very moment, or at least I hope so.
In my view, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. Minister of National Revenue was entitled to discuss the matter last Friday, I feel I would not be out of order in discussing it in general terms.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I repeat to the hon. member for St. Ann that his remarks must pertain to the vote under consideration. Otherwise, I shall have to rule him out of order, and he will have to give the floor to another hon. member.

In that case, Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be all the shorter.
It is utterly illogical to ask us to vote money for the C.B.C. at a time when most of its employees are on strike. I understand that a few employees are still at work, although certain newspapers say there are none, while others state there are some. For this reason, I wish to recall the question I directed to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) on 29 January last, as reported on page 459 of Hansard:

Supply-C.B.C.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Labour. In view of the discussions which have taken place in the last few days, is the minister now willing to intervene in the dispute between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its producers in Montreal-
The minister's reply to my question was negative.
Then, I tried again to put the question to the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) and again, the answer was negative since, I was told, the question concerned the Minister of National Revenue.
Since we are dealing now with a matter under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue, I find it odd that he should not be in the house this afternoon. In fact, he was not here at the opening of the sitting. It is unthinkable that we should be discussing a matter which concerns the Minister of National Revenue, in the absence of the minister concerned, or of the Minister of Labour. In my opinion, the strike which has already lasted 45 days is important enough to warrant the attendance here of the ministers concerned.
I wonder if it is not because only the French network is affected that the strike is lasting so long? I wonder if the government would take a similar stand if the English network were affected by a strike-
Order!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Loi-selle), but I must say that his remarks are out of order. The estimates now under consideration have nothing to do with the English or the French networks, but only with the approval of a $2,193,000 grant. So, I ask the hon. member to deal only with the estimates now before us.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I will simply repeat what I said a moment ago, that it is unthinkable that we should be called to vote $2,193,000 for an agency whose employees are on strike, and this in the absence of the minister responsible for its administration. This situation is rather odd and I believe that this government is wrong in avoiding its responsibilities with regard to the present situation at the C.B.C.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, in dealing with this subject this afternoon many matters of considerable importance were
(Mr. Loiselle.]
raised but at this time I wish to refer specifically to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanau-diere. It is true that I perhaps do not interpret the French language correctly but I gather from his remarks that he was in fact suggesting a very great saving to the C.B.C. and to the taxpayers of Canada. He suggested this be done through the abolition of live television on the French network. It is quite possible that the hon. gentleman may not like some of the performers who appear on the C.B.C., either French or English, and it is also quite possible that there are some that I do not like but I certainly do not wish to abolish from television people I do not like because I want to know what I am up against and to watch them in action.
I should like to say, that I was really amazed that such a suggestion should come forward in this committee and particularly from a member who speaks the French language. As to the matter of saving that would accrue to the C.B.C., I do not think the people of Canada, either French or English, would appreciate very much the abolition of live broadcasting on the French network and the substitution therefor of films either from this country or any other country. If that subject matter ever comes up in this house certainly I will be one who will vote against it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make in connection with this matter which are prompted by what has already been said in the debate and by what has been said on a previous occasion by the Minister of National Revenue. I would, however, feel much better, and I am sure the committee would as well, if the two ministers were in the house. I would now ask the Minister of Finance, who is leading the committee, whether it would not be advisable to have the Minister of Labour and the Minister of National Revenue, both of whom are responsible for this matter, in the chamber at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance is responsible for endeavouring to pilot these supplementary estimates through the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I noticed the other evening when I made the same request the minister at once advised me that the Minister of National Revenue was on his way down and that he would see to it that the Minister of Labour would be in his seat. In no time

at all both of them were in the house and I thanked the minister for having acceded to my request as he did. I hoped-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say anything about the Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I had hoped the same thing would happen again. I do not want to say anything derogatory about either of the ministers, but I do want to make some objective and I hope helpful suggestions. They are prompted first by what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said in reporting on the present position as he did. He made a report on which we had already obtained some intimation from the press. From what he said and from the press reports we on this side of the house believe that a definite understanding has been agreed upon between the C.B.C. and the producers, and that the only issue which now remains to be settled is the return to work of the other unions and individuals who refuse to cross the picket lines or otherwise are not in a position to go to work.
While this issue on the face of it may appear simple, it is not as simple as it does appear because a great number of artists have only individual contracts with the C.B.C. During the dispute they were not in any way able to make up their programs and to appear on television because there was no technical staff available to produce the programs. It is generally recognized now that the present dispute between the C.B.C. and the producers related to a matter of principle and that principle is the recognition of the producers association. We understand that after 48 days of the dispute the C.B.C. has now agreed that the initial claim of the producers was fully justified. As far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we agree with that part of the statement made by the Minister of National Revenue that this dispute could have been settled in 30 minutes if the C.B.C. had recognized that principle from the beginning. We, therefore, cannot blame those unions which refused, or were unable, to cross the picket lines to support the producers in their claims.
But the point that I rose to make has to do with the untenable position in which the Minister of Labour finds himself. It is said by one hon. member, namely the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, that he believes there is an understanding as between the producers and the C.B.C., and that is all to the good, but that there are other unions representing some 1,300 persons in number who are still negotiating and on behalf of whom the producers feel they should negotiate until such time as a final arrangement has been arrived at.
Supply-C.B.C.
The point I want to make is this. The Minister of Labour has refused to intervene, I say incorrectly and unjustly, but now, if an understanding has been arrived at between the producers and the C.B.C., this is an entirely different dispute which has arisen, namely that of conciliation proceedings between the 1,300 represented by those other unions and the C.B.C. He must, therefore, of necessity intervene if he wants to deal with it effectively. Therefore, if he thinks he had a reason not to interfere before, which I deny, certainly there is no reason now because the same conditions and the same circumstances do not obtain. Before, the reason for non-intervention was that the C.B.C. was an agency of the crown, following the statement originally made by the Prime Minister who felt that he should not intervene in disputes such as this. To that we answered that intervention in programming, intervention in the administration of the affairs of the C.B.C., was one thing which should be avoided but that intervention to offer the good offices of the Department of Labour to settle a dispute was an entirely different thing, and that should have been done.
Now that these circumstances and these facts no longer obtain and the matter is one outside the purview, shall I say, of management, but one dealing with 1,300 other persons who are not producers, then surely it is now an obligation of the minister to offer his good offices in order to conciliate this difficulty. The whole background of the dispute, as I have tried to describe it, now makes the return to work of those unions a very important and, may I say, in some respects perhaps a complex issue. It has been discussed now, as I understand from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, for several days without any kind of settlement having been reached. Hence we think the only solution which would put an end to this long dispute would be to refer this issue to an outside arbitrator. I again appeal to the Minister of Labour, by virtue of section 56 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, to come along and appoint an arbitrator who could settle this matter. I am confident that if the government at last decides to do that, when the arbitrator makes his recommendations all persons concerned in the dispute-and I am sure hon. members would welcome such an appointment-the matter could be resolved.
Let me say this final word to the minister. I do not want to hold up the estimates any longer. This matter has been allowed to drag too long. I am not going to lay the blame on anybody today. I want to avoid that. I say that in order to have it continue no longer-

Supply-C.B.C.
because if it is a complicated matter as to salaries and other things it might drag on for a matter of days, weeks or more-the government should appoint an arbitrator by virtue of section 56 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and the arbitrator could conciliate such matters. All those men could then go back to work and we could get on with the nation's business.

Is the Minister of Finance not going to deal with the question put by the hon. member for Laurier? He asked that in a matter of this sort the Minister of Labour and if possible the Minister of National Revenue be in their seats. The Minister of Labour was here earlier today. He undoubtedly has heavy preoccupations at the moment but those could be suspended in view of the importance of this matter. The hon. member for Laurier is entitled to receive an answer from the minister to the question he put. The Minister of Finance is a knowledgeable man. We all admit that fact. There is perhaps no one else sitting on the ministerial benches who has as wide an understanding of the problems of government. But he would be the first to admit that in the matter of labour-management relations and particularly in the matter of conciliation possibly he is less adept. On that account I think he owes it to the committee to tell us whether or not the whip will be given instructions to ask the Minister of Labour to come here in order to see whether we cannot make some progress toward the authorization of the mediation or conciliation facilities of the Department of Labour for the purpose of resolving the matter that now has been going on for over 45 days.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think the record should be allowed to remain showing that the Minister of Labour has not been in the house. He has been in the house for most of the time.

I am sorry, but I did not say that. My hon. friend is quite wrong. I was not charging the Minister of Labour with dereliction of duty. I said that he had been in the house earlier, that he was not now in the house and that undoubtedly he was out of the house for good reasons. That is what I said. I am sure that when the whip reads Hansard he will find that is what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are dealing here with supplementary estimates and have been doing so. This is the third day. It is the custom of the house on such matters for the Minister of Finance to conduct the supplementary estimates through the committee except on occasions when they are considered along with the main estimates. The item immediately under consideration

is one respecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The Minister of Labour has nothing to do with this item. If the Minister of Labour were in the house the situation would be the same for this is not an item in which the Minister of Labour would be involved.
We are dealing here with an item affecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Last Friday, a day and a half of debate ago now, I gave an explanation of this item and of how it comes about. It comes about simply because when the change was made by legislation last November in the organization of the corporation that conducts the national system the statutory provision under which the proceeds of the excise tax on receiving sets and tubes went to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was repealed and it is necessary to make an alternative provision. The amount which the committee is asked to approve is simply the equivalent amount in order that the corporation may not be deprived of its revenues. It does not mean any increase in taxation. It does not mean any increase in expenditures. It is simply a means of providing that which the corporation would have received but for the change made in the legislation last fall.
I have been asked by the hon. member for Essex East now to become involved in a debate that has been going on for two days. Mr. Chairman, if ever a subject had been discussed until it was threadbare, surely it must be this question. We have heard it discussed by every hon. member of the house who seems to have any interest, close or remote, in the subject; and it has been discussed by some members time and time again. With great respect, Mr. Chairman, may I say that we have had repetitious speeches.
I now ask this committee whether the time has not come when we can proceed with our business. We have a good many items yet to pass. Some days ago we were asked to expedite the introduction in the house for discussion of items of business relating to measures to meet the problem of unemployment. Mr. Chairman, here we have item 709 which deals with the winter works program. We are now in the position of having spent three days in discussion of an earlier item and we have not yet reached the item dealing with the winter works program. At the rate we are going I do not know how many more days will pass before we reach it. I make this appeal to hon. members. Surely this present subject has been discussed until it is threadbare. I have no intention whatever of being drawn into the kind of discussion that has been going on here this afternoon. I ask members of this

committee whether they do not think the time has come when, this subject having been so thoroughly discussed, we can pass on and make progress-

The Minister of
Labour is here in the chamber now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and transact the business that remains before us in these other items, some of which are of great importance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to say just
one word with respect to what the Minister of Finance has said and it is this. We are dealing here with an item which has to do with the operating deficit of the radio and television services. It has to do with the vote of the house for money purposes in the amount of some $2 million. While we are discussing these matters I would remind the Minister of Finance that we have the right to inquire into any phase whatever of any of these matters, notwithstanding what the minister has said.
I am glad that the Minister of Labour has come into the chamber. I should like to ask him whether he would not be good enough to reply to the suggestion which I have made. If he will allow me to do so, I will make it just as briefly as I can without being repetitious. While the minister was absent from the chamber the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George reported upon the position of the negotiations in the matter now under dispute. He stated in effect that an arrangement or at least an understanding had been arrived at between the producers and the C.B.C. but that no arrangement has been made in so far as the other unions and the C.B.C. were concerned. He went on to state that was a matter which might well take time.
The point that I made in the absence of the minister was this. If the minister had the right of non-intervention earlier-something which I deny-if he was right in saying that he should not intervene in a dispute between the C.B.C. and the producers-something which I deny-now that the dispute embraces a larger field and goes into the field of unions outside the scope of the producers and outside of management, as it were, my suggestion was that, in my opinion, it would become more difficult for the Minister of Labour to refuse to intervene in order to bring about a settlement.
I therefore made this suggestion in all sincerity, Mr. Chairman. I made this suggestion because I fear that the negotiations are going to take some time, according to the report which we have received from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George as well as press reports. I may be wrong; I
Supply-C.B.C.
hope I am wrong. But suppose the negotiations take longer than is anticipated. Is it not better to try to get these people back to work as soon as possible? The suggestion I made was that the minister give consideration to intervention in this respect, namely by the appointment of an investigator who would negotiate the present difficulties as between the 1300 people represented by the unions and the C.B.C., in the hope that the members of the unions involved could go back to work at once and then we could carry on with the nation's business. I therefore ask in all sincerity if he will not give consideration to this suggestion and, if he will do so, what is his reaction to it.

The people about whom the hon. member for Laurier is talking-I must say I am not going to point my finger at him after what he said because it would be a little dangerous-have a collective agreement, and in that collective agreement there is a provision for the airing of grievances. Whatever grievances they have in respect of this matter can be ironed out under that provision.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the minister give the terms of that provision so the house would know it?
I have not a copy of the collective agreement here.

Will the minister not enlighten the house by explaining why he feels as Minister of Labour that he cannot take any position other than the one he has taken here. How does this situation differ, for instance, from a strike involving the Canadian National Railways? In such a case the Department of Labour, after the cooling off period had ended, would use its good offices, its conciliation procedures and personnel. This strike has extended over a period of 45 days. We have been told by the minister that his stand is such that mediation through that particular vehicle is not to be employed. Now, I have restrained myself in connection with this matter.
Oh, oh.

As one who has
been interested in labour matters for a long time, and as one who has had some experience in the Department of Labour, I have restrained myself in an attempt to understand exactly what was the position of the minister. I have no doubt that if this matter were left to the Minister of Labour himself, regardless of the attitude of his colleagues, he would take precisely the steps that have been recommended by the hon. member for Laurier and that are implied in what I am

Supply-C.B.C.
now saying. He would not have intervened at the beginning. He would have allowed the process of negotiation to proceed, but having proceeded for an undue time, he would then have sought to bring the parties together, not for the purpose of imposing his view on them but for the purpose of using the facilities at his disposal and the experience of those officials to arrive at a settlement.
That is what the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George was seeking to do. Are we not now presented, as a result of the attitude of the government, with the inadequacy of the suggestions made by the government in this instance? I think that the Minister of Labour must give us an explanation of why he feels as Minister of Labour that he should not authorize his officials to act. He well remembers in the case of the railway strike how hard he worked, and how hard his officials worked, to try to bring the parties together. Finally, when they could not get together, the suggestion made by the hon. member for Laurier was adopted in that instance and an arbitrator was appointed. When the Minister of Labour sits by day after day giving an indication that he does not propose to intervene, his action I believe is open to only one interpretation. It is not because he does not want to, it is because his colleagues, for some reason or another, have taken the position that he should not.
If they have taken that position, they have put the minister in a very unenviable position and one which he does not deserve, both in terms of his record on these matters and in terms of his well-known views as to the means by which disputes of this kind are settled. I invite the minister to take advantage of the friendly attitude I have taken in this matter, and to really take unto himself a position which has been pre-empted by a private member of this house.
