If this situation is allowed to go on it gives a firm indication that this government does not understand what its obligations are in this matter.

I presume, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Essex East in making his remarks was referring to the unsettled situation respecting the 1,200 union members who have been out. I assume that because today the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George did report to this house that agreement had been reached between the producers and the C.B.C. The only point at issue remains the 1,200 people.
If he refers to that then most certainly when he talks about conciliation procedure and so on he reveals that his education in the labour department must have been very limited because the conciliation department

only comes into the matter upon the request of both parties concerned where they are negotiating a new agreement and after the termination of an old agreement.
That is not right.
This situation does not refer to the one which the hon. member for Essex East tried to convey to this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have mentioned before that the discussion must be relevant. The point which has been raised by the hon. member for Essex East and the answer made by the Minister of Labour deals directly with the administrative procedures of the Department of Labour and are not, therefore, relevant to the item under discussion. I must declare this discussion out of order, and I must ask hon. members to confine their remarks to this item 701.
Furthermore, there have been a great many repetitious speeches made for one purpose or another on this particular item. Perhaps hon. members have strayed too far afield and perhaps politics have entered into this matter. I must remind hon. members that I will immediately ask any hon. member to resume his seat if he repeats what has been said before or if he makes a speech of a repetitious nature. We must realize that we are discussing one particular item and we will never proceed with the business of this house if we do not adhere to the discussion of this item. Therefore, I ask hon. members to please be relevant. Shall item 701 carry?

In connection with the point you have just raised, Mr. Chairman, as you have pointed out we are discussing a supplementary estimate to provide $2,193,552 for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in respect of the operations of that service. With all respect I should like to suggest that anything that is going on now that interferes with that service would surely be very pertinent to this particular vote that we are called upon to make to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I think anything that interferes with the operations of the C.B.C. is relevant and pertinent to this particular vote. I take it Your Honour would not interfere with that kind of discussion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is one thing I feel I should mention. It has come about as a result of the statement which the Minister of Labour has just made in answer to the suggestion I made concerning the appointment of an investigator to deal with this dispute. If I understood him, he said that that was already provided for-I hope the minister will follow me-
I said it was reported to this house by the hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, the minister in reply to my suggestion said that provision was already made in the contract for the settlement of the dispute. I asked him if he would point to the particular clause, and he said that he did not have it. The point that I desire to make now is that the proceedings which the hon. minister refers to-
Order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I consider I have a right to make this intervention at this time, and if hon. members want to interrupt me I shall appeal to the Chair. The point I desire to make is this. While the minister is correct in saying that there are in the contract provisions for negotiation, and perhaps arbitration, I want to point out to him that that is not a grievance falling under the collective agreement. Therefore the answer which he has given does not relate to the circumstances as they are found today. I submit again with deference that the minister give consideration to the appointment of an investigator under the disputes investigation act. If he did that, then with one stroke of the pen all these people would go back to work, and that is all we are asking for.
Mr. Chairman, I have a request to make of the leader of the house at this juncture. That request is that in view of the discussion we have had, and in view of a number of questions which I would like to ask not only of the Minister of Labour but the Minister of National Revenue, this item be allowed to stand, and that while the item stands perhaps it would be possible to arrive at a satisfactory conclusion to the negotiations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, had that request been made when we reached this item last Friday, of course it would have been assented to at once. As a matter of fact, 1 even suggested to my hon. friend from Laurier then that if he wanted any variation in the order in which these items were to be called, if he would let me know we would arrange that. This item was called last Friday and was discussed here all that day. Here we are again today discussing the same matter. It has been discussed threadbare time and time again. We have had all sorts of repetitious speeches. We have gone over the same ground again and again, traversing the same subject matter. To ask the item, to stand at this stage, I think, is a most unreasonable request.
May I draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, once again to the fact that as a result of the
Supply-C.B.C.
liberties which have been taken with discussion in this debate when some members have extended it beyond the proper scope of discussion even in the face of what you have said. The fact is that we have departed from the proper basis of discussion of estimates. The proper basis for discussion of estimates, as the hon. members opposite me know, is not that we have a full-ranging debate with all members on the government benches being drawn into it. The minister in charge pilots the item through. That is what we have been trying to do here, but hon. members opposite have been endeavouring to draw some ministers into this debate in connection with matters not pertaining to the administration of their departments. With respect, I ask that hon. members recall here that we are dealing with an item affecting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is not that of the Department of Labour or some other department, but it deals with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and I ask the committee, it now having discussed this question so thoroughly, to proceed and let us get on with the other business which lies before us.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to intervene at all in this debate, and I am prompted to do so only by the lecture which has been given to the opposition by the Minister of Finance, in his characteristic style. The minister seems to forget, as he was so fond of reminding his predecessor when the minister was on this side of the house, that the ministers in this house in committee of supply are suppliants asking for money to be granted to the crown for specific purposes. The minister is asking on this item for over $2 million, which we have to vote, and which any conscientious member of this house has a perfect right to object to voting. No hon. member should be gagged, and no attempt should be made to gag him. My submission is that at the present time the service for which we are being asked to vote this money is not being given to the Canadian people. That is the point. We are being asked to vote $2 million for a service which is not being given or provided. That is the issue, and when my hon. friend from Laurier, in a very respectful way, in order to assist the government in getting on with the business-
We do not want his assistance. We can manage without him.
This almighty, all-powerful government needs no help from parliament.

The hon. member-

Supply-C.B.C.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Labour to take his seat. I must also ask all hon. members to please take their seats while-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -I am on my feet. All discussion which is not relevant to item No. 701 is completely out of order. If the debate now proceeding relates to item 701 or to the details which appear on page 5, the debate will be in order; otherwise the debate is completely out of order, and I cannot justify the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. With all due respect to the Leader of the Opposition, I must tell him that if the debate relates to the item under discussion at present such remarks will be in order. Otherwise they cannot be accepted by the chair. I must therefore ask hon. members please to take due note of the remarks I have just made, and to limit their remarks to the item under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I must ask your guidance on item 701, which deals with the operation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I take it, therefore, that any subject which concerns that operation will be in order under the grant of money we are being asked to vote?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is quite true that item 701 deals with a grant of money concerning the operations of the C.B.C. We have had in this house today debate as to whether ministers should or should not be in their seats when remarks are made to them. Speeches have been made referring to the fact that the situation would not be the same if the problem related to the English network rather than the French network. There has been debate concerning every conceivable item except the one under discussion. I repeat once again that if the remarks are confined to the item under discussion, the details of which appear on page 5, they will be in order; otherwise all speakers will be out of order.

Mr. Chairman, if I may now resume my remarks about the operation of the French television network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, for which the government is asking us to vote this money, which money we feel we should not be asked to vote until the government has made a sincere effort to get those operations resumed. It seems to me that nothing could be more relevant. Here we have a service for which millions and millions and millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money are being spent, and the service for one-third of the population of this country is at the present

time not being provided. It is our submission on this side of the house that a large part of the fault for the failure to provide that service rests upon Her Majesty's ministers, and that is the position which we have taken all along.
I submit, further, that the last time this matter was before the committee the Minister of National Revenue made a very extensive and provocative speech upon this very issue. It does seem to me that this is a strange kind of parliament in which a minister can make provocative speeches and the opposition is forbidden the right to advance arguments on the point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member from Bonavista-Twillingate speaking on a point of order or on the estimate?
I am speaking on the estimate and I am saying that for 44 days, that is to say, if my arithmetic is correct, for about one-eight of the year, this service has not-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. member that the item refers to the anticipated operating deficit of the radio and television services only. I therefore declare his present remarks out of order.

I shall go on to make some further remarks and I shall endeavour as far as my understanding will permit to bring them completely within the rules of order. Your Honour has said that this amount is for the operating deficit. I suggest to you that this amount may well prove entirely inadequate to meet the operating deficit which is likely to be incurred in connection with the French language television service because of this regrettable stoppage. As my hon. friend from St. Denis pointed out earlier today, the failure to provide these programs is depriving the C.B.C. of very considerable commercial revenues and it may well be that before the fiscal year is ended, or soon afterwards, the minister will have to come back and ask us to vote even more money for this service because of the failure of the government to do anything about this problem during the last 44 days. That is surely the point, and surely it is completely relevant to the question before the house. It does not matter that the minister, or one of the ministers, by recommending a change in the law last year has put the Minister of Finance in the embarrassing position of having to ask us to vote this money. The government is responsible to parliament and is answerable for this service and it is the duty of this government to answer the question raised by members who have been elected by the people.

I did not take any part in this debate earlier because the subject is of no direct concern to me, and of even less concern to my constituents but it does seem to me that a very important point of principle has arisen here this afternoon and I say again that I feel it would be in the interest of parliament, in the interest of good government and in the interest of good order if the minister would reconsider the very reasonable request made by the hon. member for Laurier and agree to have this item stand over now in the hope that within the next 24 or 48 hours this regrettable situation can be ended. I am sure that if this were to happen there would be no further discussion of this item. I join with the hon. member for Laurier in an appeal to the minister to be conciliatory for once. Let him be reasonable for once and allow this item to stand so that we may proceed with the other urgent business the minister is at least as anxious as we are to complete.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Labour in connection with this matter. Is the Minister of Labour in a position to confirm the statement which has been made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George concerning the present position of the negotiations?
I am accepting the report of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and I heard it in the same way as the hon. gentleman did.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the hon. minister for that answer. May I pursue the matter a little further and ask him this: in view of the fact that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has stated that there seems to be an understanding between the C.B.C. and the producers, and that the other matter is under negotiation, will the Minister of Labour now give consideration to intervening with regard to the latter part of the dispute?
What for?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like an answer to that question.

As I have tried to explain, there is an existing collective agreement between those people who are affected and the C.B.C., and there is provision in such agreement for the appropriate procedure to be followed. This is one of the things which can be taken up with the management in an effort to reach a solution. At a later date, after there has been a return to work and
Supply-C.B.C.
efforts have been made to iron out an agreement, if a request is made to the Department of Labour for someone to sit in on the discussions in order to help bring about a settlement there would be no objection.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But I am informed by the minister's own officials that the procedure which the minister has just outlined applies to the contract which was signed heretofore but does not apply to the present dispute; in other words, there is a new dispute and therefore the suggestion which the minister has made does not apply. Is that correct or not?

I still do not know whether the hon. gentleman understands which contract he is discussing. Is he talking about the collective agreement between the 1,200 members of the staff who refused to pass the picket line, or is he talking about the agreement between the producers and the C.B.C.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am talking about the former and not the latter. I said that clearly in my earlier remarks. That is the matter in which the minister has already stated he would not interfere. With reference to the other matter-that concerning the 1,300 employees-I was saying that since this is a matter between the C.B.C. and its staff it is in a different position from that which he stated, and would he not now give consideration to intervention in the latter part of the dispute.
I have already said that to my knowledge there is an existing collective agreement and there are provisions in this agreement for the settlement of this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have a number of questions I should like to put to the Minister of National Revenue, but he is not now here and I am appealing to the leader of the government now to allow this matter to stand for the purpose I have mentioned earlier.

Mr. Chairman, had the Minister of National Revenue been here I should have liked to have commented on the speech he made on this subject last Friday. At that time he made a comprehensive statement in committee on this particular estimate as reported on pages 775, 776, 777, and 778 of Hansard. In the course of this statement-and no one objected to its being made-the minister referred to the circumstances under which the strike arose and referred to certain features in connection with it. He said, as reported on page 777, that he intended to give something of the background to this strike and, indeed, he went into great detail. We

Supply-C.B.C.
thought that was quite a proper thing to do, though we might not have agreed with what the minister said.
This statement aroused a great deal of interest on this side of the house and we had looked forward to asking some questions and making some comments with regard to it. Unfortunately the minister is not here this afternoon. With regard to one of the matters about which I should have liked to have inquired perhaps the Minister of Finance could be helpful. In any case, he might be able to pass the question on to his colleague. My question is this: whether the strike has resulted in a loss of revenue to the C.B.C. and in an increase of expenditure by the C.B.C. to such a point-as was suggested by my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate a few moments ago-that an additional supplementary estimate may be required. That surely is a very reasonable question to ask the minister in connection with an estimate of this magnitude for the operations of the C.B.C. which are so seriously affected by this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be quite impossible to say now what will be the eventual effect on the revenues or expenditures of the corporation as a result of this strike. Suffice it to say that the amount the committee is asked to appropriate here is the amount it has already appropriated at the last session of parliament, has already approved both in principle and in amount. The committee is not asked to provide any money additional to what it has previously provided nor to approve any departure in principle from that which the committee has already approved on a previous occasion.

Before this item is carried, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could state to the committee what portion of the sum of $2,193,552 is spent to cover salaries of the employees of the C.B.C. and also what portion is spent to cover salaries of the producers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not possible to break this item down in this fashion any more than the preceding item was broken down. As my hon. friend will have no trouble in learning by reference to the estimates introduced in the last session, this is a block item. It is applied to the entire operation of the C.B.C., its operation of the national network service, both radio and television. I have already explained that this item is one already voted by the house under the general provisions of the statute under which the revenues from the excise tax on radio receiving sets and tubes went to the corporation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: More obstruction.

My hon. friend says, "more obstruction". Does my hon. friend think that is the way he is going to encourage us to accept his suggestions? We are a small group on this side of the house but my hon. friend may be certain of one thing, that no suggestion from the ministerial benches to the effect that we are obstructing simply because we seek to assert our rights is going to further progress in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have had two days of it already.

We on this side cannot be accused of obstructionism simply because we seek to do our duty. My hon. friend is the last man in this house who should say that.
The Leader of the Opposition has pointed out that the Minister of National Revenue made an extended statement on this matter covering all aspects of the strike and giving his interpretation of it. The Leader of the Opposition said that he would like to have had the opportunity of putting questions to the Minister of National Revenue arising out of that statement and the hon. member for Laurier took that position, too. I would urge the Minister of Finance in a moment now of deep conciliation and understanding to accept the suggestion of these two hon. gentlemen. We have questions to put on this matter. Can my hon. friend tell us when we will have an opportunity of putting further questions and receiving answers to those questions. He asks us to help him and dispose of this item. We are not unwilling to help him provided we are given an opportunity of complying with what we think in this matter is our duty. What opportunity will be afforded us to put further questions? If this item passes there will be no opportunity except on orders of the day of putting questions to the ministers and under the practices of this house they will have the right, if they want, to refuse to answer.
In the absence of a willingness to let this item stand the hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that this request to us is one that cannot possibly be accepted by any responsible opposition doing its duty. I ask the Minister of Finance again if he does not think he will further the passage of his supplementary estimates by acceding to the request of the hon. member for Laurier?
I invite the Minister of Finance to remember one occasion when passing my own estimates I was confronted with almost

exactly this situation and I persisted in refusing the request of my hon. friend to place before the house certain statements about estimated and actual expenditures. He will recall that occasion and he will also recall how finally, having made the mistake that he is now making I acceded to the request and the result was that my estimates were passed very quickly. I ask my hon. friend to remember that particular occasion and to accede to the request put by the hon. member for Laurier. If the minister fails to do so he forces us into the position of continuing this discussion as the only means by which we can hold this matter open to give us an opportunity of discussing a question which is of the greatest importance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to discuss the questions I have to direct to the Minister of National Revenue. Because he is not in this place and in order to establish the basis for them I shall have to refer back to the statement made by the Minister of National Revenue as reported at page 776 of Hansard of February 6, 1959, when he gave the impression that the producers walked out on the C.B.C. The minister said on that occasion:
Then on December 29, at nine o'clock in the morning, a conference started between representatives of the producers and the representatives of management and that conference went on during the day. There were breaks for discussion with the principals, breaks for luncheon, of course, and all the rest of it. Then at five o'clock in the afternoon the picket lines were marching around the C.B.C. building. The ultimate weapon, the last weapon, the last weapon that should have been used, was brought into play on the first day.
And the strike started. What I would like to ask the minister is if he has seen the brief prepared by the producers which was placed in the boxes of all hon. members of parliament and which deals with this very subject, not in the manner in which the minister dealt with it but in an entirely different manner. I shall not take the time of the committee as I very well could by reading what is contained at page 5 of the brief but I shall summarize it in this fashion.
The brief clearly states the manner in which the negotiations and the proceedings leading up to the last negotiation were brought to an end. The brief states that the first interview between the producers and the C.B.C. took place on December 11. The brief goes on to indicate that a second meeting occurred on December 19 and a third on December 20. They met again on December 23 and Mr. Andre Ouimet was informed of the result of the secret vote authorizing the producers to interrupt the work. The brief states there was no answer to that communication until December 29 when, after 66968-9-59
Supply-C.B.C.
a long meeting with no progress being made, it was then decided to walk out.
The question I ask the minister is this. In view of the statement which he made at page 776 of Hansard has he not taken cognizance of page 5 of this brief which is a complete answer to his statement and will he not make a statement to the house at the first opportunity dealing with that part of his remarks?
Later on in the course of his remarks the minister stated that if top management at Ottawa had been advised the strike would have been settled in thirty minutes. According to the information I have at my disposal, and which again is to be found in the brief, it is quite true to say that top management of the C.B.C. in Ottawa were not properly informed of the situation which had developed in Montreal during the month of December. But it would have been improper for the producers to bypass the C.B.C. officials in Montreal and make contact with top management in Ottawa.
The next question I would like to ask the minister is this:	Is it not a fact that in
view of his statement he would have considered it quite improper for those people in Montreal to refuse to talk or to give the result of their discussions with C.B.C. officials in Montreal instead of coming on to deal with top management, as he said, here in Ottawa? If top management in Ottawa was not informed of the situation, then I have only one conclusion to come to and it is that the local management in Montreal is the one which perhaps should be blamed for the producers being here.
I would like to get the reaction of the minister to my question. It would seem to me that the conduct of those who were dealing with the Montreal group was right, and it was proper for them to continue to deal with the Montreal group. On the contrary, it would have been most improper for them to somersault or jump over the Montreal group and come to Ottawa for discussions unless, of course, they had been invited so to do by the minister. Therefore, I invite the minister to comment on this second point.
There is another question which I should like to address to the minister because he said on a number of occasions that the producers knew full well what they should have done. He made it quite clear that they should have gone to the labour relations board and there get certified in the usual way. I could get the reference to that in Hansard very quickly if need be, but I want to point out to the minister that there are at least two unions in the C.B.C. which have not been

Supply-C.B.C.
certified by the labour relations board but which have been recognized by the C.B.C. through direct negotiations. Therefore, there is no point in making an exception of the producers by saying to them, "You have to go to the board". In the face of that situation, I ask the minister why he should direct the statement which he did to the C.B.C. when there are, as I say, at least two other unions in the same position.
I come back to the original submission which I made, Mr. Chairman. I ask the Minister of Finance to reconsider the answer which he has given in order that we might have an opportunity to ask further questions if we so desire and I suggest to him once again that he allow this item to stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 701 carry?
I would like to ask a few questions but I would like the minister to answer the questions of the hon. member for Laurier first.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These matters have all been dealt with; they have been discussed in this debate many times. My hon. friend is just asking me to say things that have been said before and to open up this matter all over again. I must decline with thanks.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The three questions which were asked are three new questions arising out of the discussion which took place the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They may look new to my hon. friend but I doubt whether they look new to the majority of the members of this committee.
Can the minister inform the house what portion of this grant of $2 million odd is to cover the deficit of the French television network in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have already explained that matter very fully. I am sorry if my hon. friend was not in the house or did not follow what I said. It was made perfectly clear.

Mr. Chairman, surely they must have some records to show what the deficit was in Montreal for the month of January,
1958,	compared with the month of January,
1959,	so we can get an idea of the consequences of the strike we are discussing. After all, we are passing an item to cover a deficit. We would like to know whether the deficit will be higher this month than it was last month. Maybe we will be short of money; if the strike lasts for months and months how far will this amount of money take you?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was all discussed half an hour ago.

Mr. Chairman, we have this afternoon a minister who is refusing to answer questions asked by members on this side of the house. The fact that this item was voted at the last session does not justify the minister in refusing to give us information which we want now. Conditions have changed since the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation were discussed in this house. Conditions today are certainly different from what they were then. At the present time a certain number of French producers are on strike. It is unfortunate that the minister responsible for the C.B.C. is not here this afternoon to answer these questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You know he is ill, don't you?

I have other questions to ask. If he is ill that is one more reason why this item should be allowed to stand. It is not fair to hon. members to ask this committee to vote over $2 million without any information as to what this amount of money will cover. I repeat, the fact that we did not ask for these details at the last session is no justification for the position taken by the minister. I know that the minister said a few days ago-and he repeated it today-we are talking about everything under the sun in order to prevent reaching a discussion of the winter works program. Mr. Chairman, when such an attitude is taken by a minister of the crown, a member of a government whose Prime Minister is the advocate of a bill of rights, I say it is not right. We have a right to get information and that is what we are trying to do this afternoon, and information is being refused us.
You don't want any information.

A remark was made on the other side of the house that I do not want information. I have a question which I wanted to ask the Minister of National Revenue. We are voting money for the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Last July or August the minister announced in this house that steps were being taken to extend the French television network to Moncton and to certain other sections of New Brunswick. I wanted to find out at this time what progress had been made. We understand we are to be advised that nothing has been done in this regard. I think we have the right to get some information.

I have one question to ask the Minister of Finance. I should like to know why he refuses to allow this item to

stand. I think the opposition members have a right to an answer to the questions they have put to the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of National Revenue. They have put them in a constructive way.
Oh, oh.

I hear some
laughter. We are getting accustomed to hearing members on the government side laugh when we discuss some very important problems in this house. I was here in 1956 when a certain debate took place in this house and the one member who was the most critical about the rights of parliament being not treated very well by the government was precisely the one who is today the Minister of Finance in this house. I should like him to answer my question if he cares to do so. Why would he not allow this item to stand until the Minister of National Revenue comes back to the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I suppose this discussion can go on and on in this way if my hon. friends want to keep on spinning it out. The fact is that the reasons have already been given and, in my opinion, in a reasonable manner. We have had two days' discussion on this matter. We have been over all these matters and we are just going over them again.
We have received no answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Having regard to the important business that is waiting to be done, my hon. friend wants to keep this thing going indefinitely. He says the matter should be left over and kept going indefinitely.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, he does not ask that; he asks that the item be allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We must get some other items passed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Let it stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I thought I was asked a question by another hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There will be
plenty of opportunities for the discussion of C.B.C. matters during the course of the session when we come to the estimates for the next year and whatever steps are taken for the annual review of C.B.C. operations. There will be plenty of opportunity then for hon. members to go into these matters to their heart's content. But so far as this present item is concerned, we have had the explanation given time and again as to what it is for. Hon. members understand it perfectly 66968-9-59i

well. But there is a desire to discuss something else and to keep this thing going. I cannot prevent hon. members from keeping it going if they want to do so, Mr. Chairman. But I appeal to the good sense of the committee and ask hon. members to have regard to the fact that nothing new is coming out of this discussion and that no good purpose is to be served by keeping a discussion like this open endlessly simply by repetition. The questions that have been asked in search of information have been answered. The committee is fully in possession of the information relevant to this item. I think hon. members are aware of this fact. I can only repeat the appeal that I made earlier, namely that we proceed with the important business which is waiting to be done and which is being held up in the meantime.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I quite understand that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), being ill, could not answer our questions today. Nevertheless, we simply claim the right-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) that if he wishes to speak, he must do so from his place.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is necessary to do so when the house is in committee, but since you insist, I will go back to my desk, if you will give me a minute to do so.
Mr. Chairman being back to my seat, I must say that we are sorry that the Minister of National Revenue is not in the house at this moment to answer our questions. All we ask is that the government let us wait until the hon. minister's return, before we approve this important item, before we vote millions of dollars to the C.B.C., without having the information we are asking for.
There are three questions I should like to ask-
(Text):

Will the hon. member permit a question? In a prior speech in this debate the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville said that he had received a number of letters concerning the desirability of the government's intervening in this matter. (Translation):

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell the Minister of Finance who intervened just a moment ago that I make one final appeal to him.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If the committee will allow me to continue, perhaps they will not regret my intervention at this time. I make this last appeal because, as the hon. member for Gloucester has said, the Minister of National Revenue is ill. It is only fair to ask the present leader of the government to allow the item to stand and to go to the bottom of the list so that we may discuss other items in the meantime. He may find that the progress made with the others will be satisfactory.
If the minister does not wish to accede to my request may I say this. I see the Prime Minister coming into the chamber now. I make the request to him also. If the request is not acceded to, I am saying now to the minister and to the committee that we shall have no other alternative than to allow the item to pass, making it quite clear, however, that we have done our best, in fact our utmost, to obtain answers to questions from both the Minister of Labour and, particularly, the Minister of National Revenue who is not here. I repeat in the presence of the Prime Minister the request which I have made, namely that the matter be allowed to stand until the Minister of National Revenue returns. If the answer is to be in the negative, I say what I said earlier, namely that we will not delay the item any further.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the reference to the absence of the Minister of
[Mr. Dupuis.1
National Revenue as a result of illness comes as an afterthought in this matter. It was some time ago, without any reference to that fact, that the hon. member for Laurier proposed that this item stand. We have spent two long days on this item. I do not think it is going to be any effective contribution to orderly debate or to the transaction of the business of the house just to leave this matter open so that it can be started all over again on another day. I repeat the appeal that I have made to the committee, namely that we proceed with the important business of the committee that is urgently waiting to be done and that we do not go on with this endless repetition when the committee has already been given all the information that is required and is relevant.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the Minister of Finance that for two days we have been discussing this item and that for two days we have been asking for information. But it is also true that for two days we have never had any answers to satisfy the public and the hon. members. While the minister is anxious that this item be passed, may I ask what is the urgency? If the Minister of Finance is not in a position to answer questions in place of the Minister of National Revenue, why do we not get the officials here with the books and something we can rely upon? The Minister of Finance is here trying to answer questions. He has not the books. He has no notes. He has no officials with him. He has no information. He has no answers. Nevertheless he thinks we are discussing the matter to no purpose. If there is some urgent matter to be discussed after this item is disposed of, why do we not allow this item to stand and go on with the more urgent questions?
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance a question. I should like to know what proportion of the amount to be voted would be spent for the French network.
Oh, oh.
Surely the minister must have some idea of how much money would be voted for the French network. Surely he can tell us at least approximately.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, you will recall, even if the hon. member does not, that I answered that question about one hour ago.
What was the answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) cannot answer our questions, I suggest that we let the matter stand until the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) returns to the house, because these are matters of public interest that must be raised at this time. Moreover, I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that we cannot make other inquiries until the Minister of Finance has replied to the inquiries we have already made, or until the Minister of National Revenue has been able to reply to the questions put to him by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier).
I also submit that the opposition has a right, particularly at this time, when a strike is affecting the staff of the French network of the C.B.C., to ask questions of the government and to expect definite answers which will be satisfactory to the people that we represent in this house.
Consequently, I would ask the Minister of Finance to give us, in the opposition, the right to ask questions of the Minister of National Revenue when he is well again; in short, we are simply asking that he adjourn this item until the hon. Minister of National Revenue can answer the very important questions that were put to him today.
I trust that the Minister of Finance who, when he sat with the opposition often called for fair play, will allow us to put our questions, and if he cannot give the answers, he will agree to wait for the return of the Minister of National Revenue.

703. Contribution to the Springhill disaster relief fund, 1958, $100,000.

This is the item having
to do with the contribution to the Springhill disaster fund, Mr. Chairman. In the absence of the Leader of the Opposition, 1 should like to say that we are heartily in accord with what the government is doing and give it our warmest approval. While I know the Minister of Finance might be technical and tell me that it would be out of order, may I ask him if the government, in consultation with the government of Nova Scotia, has
Supply-Finance
made any advance in its plans for the permanent rehabilitation of Springhill? If the minister has any information he could impart to the house I am sure all members on both sides would be interested in having it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there is
no information additional to that which has already been communicated to the house.

I want to say, on behalf of
this group, that we, like the official opposition, approve of this action.
What group? Is one a group?

Has the government any
plans for rehabilitation or is it working in co-operation with the municipality or any organization in that area with respect to rehabilitation of those who suffered as a result of the disaster at Springhill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There will be an
opportunity for my hon. friend to go into that question in due course when the estimates of the proper department are before the committee. This item simply concerns a contribution the government proposes to make, and asks the house to approve, to the disaster fund. Other questions can be raised later in the session on the estimates.

I wonder if the minister
could just assist us by telling us what would be the proper department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mines and technical surveys.

I should like to say a few
words on this item since I am the representative for Springhill. I should like to take this opportunity to thank the Minister of Finance, and through him the government of Canada, for this very substantial donation to this enormous fund which was built up for the wives and families of the victims of this tragic disaster in Springhill. At the same time, I should like to thank the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Kootenay West for their interest. I should like to say once again, as I said before, that I am glad at last the official opposition is showing some concern for the people of Springhill and their problems.

I do not think we could allow that last remark by the hon. member for Cumberland to pass. It is well known that no one expressed sooner or in stronger terms his support for the people of Springhill than my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition.

I should like to put a few words on the record concerning this grant

Supply-Finance
to the Springhill disaster relief fund. I would associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for Cumberland in the throne speech debate, and also the remarks made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. I am well acquainted with this town of Springhill since I lived there for some time and went to high school there. My father was for 4 years the manager of No. 4 mine which suffered an explosion just two years earlier than this terrible bump which took place last year. The towns of Springhill and Westville, another mining town in the county of Pictou, are very much alike. A few years before the explosion in 1956 in Springhill we suffered an explosion in the McGregor mine in Pictou county, and at that time some 39 miners lost their lives. I lost some of own relatives at that time.
The people of the two towns are, of course, rugged. The people of Canada had their eyes upon Springhill, and I am sure that the grant will be passed by this parliament. As far as the rehabilitation of Springhill is concerned, I will not go into that. As was pointed out by the Minister of Finance, we will have an opportunity to speak on that matter when the estimates of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys are under consideration. I may say that men from my own county went as draegermen to assist in Springhill, as did the men from Cape Breton.
I am sure that in the future, as indicated by actions today, there will be co-operation between the federal government and the government of Nova Scotia and everything will be done to help Springhill. I know that there was not too much done after the explosion in the McGregor mine about four or five years ago for the county of Pictou by way of assistance from either the federal or provincial governments. However I have the utmost faith in our federal government of today, and also in our present provincial government in Nova Scotia.
